claims.text: At approximately 0.5 Tm under sustained loading, FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy multilayers with intact BCC short-range order exhibit progressive plastic deformation.
Dislocations are generated preferentially in the FCC layers.
Dislocations accumulate at incoherent FCC/BCC interfaces.
Dislocation accumulation produces high local interfacial stresses that trigger localized SRO relaxation in adjacent BCC layers.
Localized SRO relaxation lowers the barrier for dislocation transmission across the FCC/BCC interfaces.
The reduced transmission barrier causes the creep rate to accelerate progressively.
Moderate sub-recrystallization annealing partially disrupts SRO in the BCC layers.
Pre-disrupted SRO provides a lower and more nearly constant barrier to dislocation motion.
Pre-disrupted SRO produces a more uniform creep rate with a less pronounced temporal change.
The proposed coating consists of alternating FCC CoCrFeMnNi-type and complementary BCC high-entropy-alloy layers.
The individual layers are approximately 30–50 nm thick.
Rapid cooling maintains a high degree of SRO in the BCC layers.
FCC/BCC interfaces and BCC-layer SRO jointly mediate dislocation nucleation, pile-up, and transmission.
The FCC/BCC interfaces act as primary barriers to dislocation motion.
Reducing layer thickness promotes earlier interaction between dislocations and interfaces.
Reducing layer thickness lowers the total strain at which SRO relaxation and associated creep acceleration begin.
Relative to rapidly cooled intact-SRO samples, annealed samples will show less progressive creep and a more constant creep rate.
Similar creep progression and interfacial dislocation dynamics in intact-SRO and pre-disrupted-SRO samples would falsify the proposed SRO-relaxation mechanism.
